title: The man on the road
hookLine: Upaka the wanderer hears him, shakes his head, and takes another road (MN 26)

lines: A LONG WALK TO THE FIVE.
cards: Not every first meeting goes well. A pitch gets a polite nod. A favorite song gets a shrug and a huh, good for you.
The subject changes, and that's that. The Buddha has decided to teach. He's thought about who should hear first, and he's chosen his five old companions, the ones who left him when he ate.
They're in a deer park near Varanasi, a long walk away. So he sets out on the road, and not far along it, he meets a stranger.

teach.b: The stranger is Upaka, a wanderer too, from a group called the Ajivikas, and he's struck by what he sees. Your face is so clear, friend, he says, your skin so bright. Who's your teacher?
Whose teaching do you follow? It's an open door. The Buddha answers, the sutta says, in verse.
He says he has no teacher; he found this himself.

He has overcome everything, understood everything, and he's on his way to Kasi to set the wheel of the teaching turning, to beat the drum of the deathless in a world gone blind. It's a big answer. Upaka listens.
Then he says something like: may it be so, friend.

teach.h: MAY IT BE SO. A SIDE ROAD.
teach.b: He shakes his head, takes a side road, and walks away. That's it. The stranger doesn't buy it.
The Buddha tells this story himself, and doesn't hide it. He doesn't chase Upaka. He doesn't argue.
He just keeps walking to the deer park. The later tradition adds a coda.
The commentary's story goes that Upaka fell in love and married a hunter's daughter named Capa, had a son, and later, unhappy, went looking for the Buddha after all, and became a monk.
Capa's own verses survive in the Therigatha, the poems of the early nuns. So the man on the road wasn't lost.

how: Buddhists retell Upaka's meeting as a reminder not to force the teaching on anyone, and in some traditions teachers wait to be asked before they teach, letting people come and go freely.

o: the first of the five monks at the Deer Park
a wanderer who heard the Buddha and walked away
the Buddha's own teacher before the awakening

games.q: who's on the road — tap the pairs.
p: shook his head and took a side road

s: Upaka became the Buddha's follower on the spot
Upaka said may it be so, shook his head, and took another road.
the Buddha told the Upaka story about himself, failure and all
in MN 26, without hiding that the first listener walked away.
the Buddha chased Upaka to change his mind
he kept walking to the deer park.

games.q: you're Upaka. a wanderer with a shining face tells you he's found the deathless with no teacher at all. what do you do?
o: say may it be so, shake your head, and take a side road.
games.why: Upaka takes the side road. the stranger doesn't believe. and the Buddha doesn't chase him.

practice: Think of someone who disagrees with you about something that matters to you, small, like a movie, or big, like how to live, and picture them shaking their head and walking off down a side road.
Notice what rises, the urge to chase, to argue, to prove, and let it be there. Then gently let them go, wish them well on their road, and keep walking yours.

wordCard.voice: Upaka. The wanderer who asked the Buddha about his teaching, then said may it be so, shook his head, and took another road.

orig.note: Pali: an Ajivika, a member of the wandering group Upaka belonged to.

carryVoice: Your line: not everyone is ready. The road to the deer park goes on. Sixty days, well walked.

sources.ref: Ariyapariyesana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 26): the meeting with Upaka
